problem_text: In each square of a garden shaped like a 2022×2022 board, there is initially a tree of height 0. A gardener and a lumberjack alternate turns playing the following game, with the gardener taking the first turn: The gardener chooses a square in the garden. Each tree on that square and all the surrounding squares (of which there are at most eight) then becomes one unit taller. The lumberjack then chooses four different squares on the board. Each tree of positive height on those squares then becomes one unit shorter. We say that a tree is majestic if its height is at least 10^6. Determine the largest K such that the gardener can ensure there are eventually K majestic trees on the board, no matter how the lumberjack plays.
solution_text: The gardener adds +1 to a 3×3 block (up to 9 trees) per turn, while the lumberjack subtracts -1 from 4 squares per turn. The net growth rate is 5 per round. If the gardener cycles uniformly through all N = 2022² = 4,088,484 squares, each interior tree gets growth rate 9/N per round. The lumberjack can distribute 4 decrements per round. If the lumberjack focuses on k trees, each gets decrement rate 4/k per round. A tree grows iff 9/N > 4/k, i.e., k > 4N/9. So the lumberjack can suppress at most floor(4N/9) trees, and the gardener guarantees ceil(5N/9) = 5 × 4,088,484 / 9 = 2,271,380 majestic trees. The bound is tight: the lumberjack can achieve 4N/9 suppression by targeting the same set of 4N/9 trees every round, giving each a suppression rate of 9/N, exactly canceling the gardener's growth.
solution_summary: Rate argument: gardener adds 9/round, lumberjack removes 4/round, net 5/round. Uniform cycling gives each tree 9/N growth rate. Lumberjack can suppress at most 4N/9 trees. Gardener guarantees 5N/9 = 2271380 majestic trees. Bound is tight via adversarial lumberjack strategy.
